claims.text: The starting eutectic CoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure consisting of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and exhibits brittle behavior.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal boundaries cause local stress concentrations, microcracking, and brittleness during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Annealing at approximately 600 °C for 1 hour under an inert atmosphere, followed by controlled cooling, will modify the alloy beneficially.
The specified annealing treatment induces fine nanoscale precipitates at the internal lamellar boundaries.
The annealing-induced nanoscale precipitates are coherent with the surrounding material.
The boundary precipitates act as dislocation sinks.
The precipitates reduce dislocation accumulation and associated stress concentrations at lamellar interfaces.
The nanoscale precipitates provide precipitation hardening.
Precipitation hardening will retain or increase the alloy's tensile strength.
The treated alloy will have significantly greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy will have greater resistance to microcracking than the untreated alloy.
The treated alloy's strength will be retained or slightly increased relative to the untreated alloy.
The beneficial strength-ductility response depends on retaining nanoscale, coherent precipitates and avoiding overaging.
Annealing or cooling deviations that cause precipitate coarsening or loss of coherency could eliminate the ductility benefit.
